target: ज़रा एक टैक्सी बुक कर दो।
english: Just book a taxi.
tip: ज़रा (zara = just a little) softens a command the way English 'just' does: ज़रा एक टैक्सी बुक कर दो (zara ek taxi book kar do) sounds friendly, not bossy.

target: ज़रा धीरे बोलिए, सबको सुनाई नहीं दे रहा।
english: Please speak softly, people can't hear.
tip: Being heard is phrased with देना (dena = give): सुनाई नहीं दे रहा (sunai nahin de raha) = literally 'not giving to hearing' = can't be heard. Seeing works the same: दिखाई देना (dikhai dena).

target: भैया, दो किलो प्याज़ दे दीजिए।
english: Brother, please give two kilos of onions.
tip: भैया (bhaiya = brother) is the normal way to address a shopkeeper you don't know – Hindi uses family words for friendly strangers, so no name needed.

target: चलो शोभा, बाहर चलकर ताज़ी हवा लेते हैं।
english: Come Shobha, let's go outside and get fresh air.
tip: चलो (chalo = let's go) opens a 'let's' suggestion, then the verb stays plain: ताज़ी हवा लेते हैं (taazi hawa lete hain) = 'we take fresh air', meaning let's.

target: छाता साथ ले लो, बारिश हो सकती है।
english: Take an umbrella along, it might rain.
tip: A helper लो (lo, from लेना = take) marks the action as for your own benefit: छाता साथ ले लो (chhata saath le lo) = take the umbrella along, for yourself. Acting for others uses दो (do) instead.

target: बैंक जाकर पासबुक अपडेट करा लो।
english: Go to the bank and get the passbook updated.
tip: करा (kara) means someone else does it: पासबुक अपडेट करा लो (passbook update kara lo) = get it updated – the clerk does the work, not you.

target: क्या आपकी शादी हो चुकी है?
english: Are you already married?
tip: चुकना (chukna) is a whole verb meaning 'already done': हो चुकी है (ho chuki hai) = has already happened. Hindi needs no separate word for 'already'.

target: श्याम अपना सामान उठा ले गया।
english: Shyam picked up his stuff and left.
tip: उठा ले गया (utha le gaya) stacks three verbs – picked-took-went. ले जाना (le jaana = take-go) is carrying something away; ले आना (le aana) is bringing it.

target: बच्चे ने सारा खाना खा लिया।
english: The child ate up all the food.
tip: खा लिया (kha liya) adds लेना (lena = take) to 'eat' – the action lands on yourself, fully finished. Plain खाया (khaya) = ate; खा लिया = ate it all up.

target: चाय ठंडी हो गई।
english: The tea got cold.
tip: ठंडी हो गई (thandi ho gayi) = 'became cold, gone' – जाना (jaana = go) after a verb stamps the change as complete. The tea isn't cooling; it's already cold.

target: बस अभी-अभी निकल गई।
english: The bus just left.
tip: Doubling a word tightens it in Hindi: अभी (abhi) = now, अभी-अभी (abhi-abhi) = just this instant. The bus is barely out of sight.

target: ट्रेन छूट गई।
english: I missed the train.
tip: ट्रेन छूट गई (train chhoot gayi) = 'the train slipped away' – the train is the subject, not you. Hindi reports the mishap with no 'I' taking the blame.

target: निशा ने एक रात में पूरी किताब पढ़ डाली।
english: Nisha read through the entire book in one night.
tip: पढ़ डाली (padh daali) tacks डालना (daalna = throw) onto 'read' – the flavor is doing it in one intense sweep. A whole book in one night earns डाली.

target: सुरेश अचानक रो पड़ा।
english: Suresh suddenly burst into tears.
tip: रो पड़ा (ro pada) puts पड़ना (padna = fall) after 'cry' – it marks a sudden, uncontrolled burst. Suresh didn't decide to cry; the tears just came.

target: मैंने उसे मैसेज भेज दिया।
english: I sent him the message.
tip: भेज दिया (bhej diya) ends in देना (dena = give) – the action moves away from you, toward someone else. Its mirror is लेना (lena) for actions done for yourself.

target: जो पढ़ेगा, वो आगे बढ़ेगा।
english: One who studies will progress.
tip: English says 'one who studies'; Hindi puts the future in both halves: जो पढ़ेगा, वो आगे बढ़ेगा (jo parhega, vo aage barhega = who will study, he will move ahead).

target: जहाँ-जहाँ पानी है, वहाँ-वहाँ जीवन है।
english: Wherever there is water, there is life.
tip: Doubling spreads the meaning: जहाँ-जहाँ... वहाँ-वहाँ (jahaan-jahaan... vahaan-vahaan = in each place... in each such place). Single जहाँ (jahaan) = where; doubled = every single place.

target: जो किताब तुमने दी, वह बहुत अच्छी थी।
english: The book that you gave was very good.
tip: Hindi doesn't embed 'that you gave' – it leads with it: जो किताब तुमने दी (jo kitaab tumne di = which book you gave), then वह (vah = that) restarts the sentence.

target: जो मेहनत करता है वही सफल होता है।
english: The one who works hard is the one who succeeds.
tip: वही (vahi) is वह + ही: जो मेहनत करता है वही (jo mehnat karta hai vahi = who works hard, that one exactly) succeeds – the ही adds 'and nobody else'.

target: जिस दिन बारिश हुई, उस दिन स्कूल बंद था।
english: The day it rained, school was closed that day.
tip: Hindi names the noun twice: जिस दिन... उस दिन (jis din... us din = which day... that day). English says 'the day it rained' once – Hindi echoes it in both halves.

target: जिस कमरे में हम बैठे थे, वहाँ बहुत गर्मी थी।
english: The room where we were sitting was very hot.
tip: जो (jo = which) bends before a position word, like who–whom: जिस कमरे में (jis kamre mein = in which room). When में, से or पर follows, singular jo becomes jis.

target: जो भी यहाँ आता है, उसे यह जगह पसंद आती है।
english: Whoever comes here likes this place.
tip: Add भी (bhi = even) to जो and 'who' becomes 'whoever': जो भी यहाँ आता है (jo bhi yahaan aata hai = whoever comes here). The same trick works on where and when words.

target: जैसा अमित ने बताया, वैसा ही हुआ।
english: It happened exactly as Amit told.
tip: जैसा अमित ने बताया, वैसा ही हुआ (jaisa Amit ne bataya, vaisa hi hua = the way Amit said, exactly that way it happened) – English drops the 'that way' half; Hindi keeps it.

target: जिसके पास ज्ञान है, उसके पास ताक़त है।
english: One who has knowledge, has power.
tip: Hindi has no verb 'have' – owning sits near you: जिसके पास ज्ञान है (jiske paas gyaan hai = near whom knowledge is) means 'whoever has knowledge'.

target: रूबी ने जो काम शुरू किया था, वह आख़िरकार पूरा हो ही गया।
english: The work Ruby started is finally done.
tip: पूरा हो ही गया (poora ho hi gaya = did finally get done): slipping ही (hi) inside the verb adds 'at last, despite everything'. Without it, the work just got done – no relief.

target: परीक्षा रद्द कर दी गई।
english: The exam was cancelled.
tip: One English word, three Hindi verbs: रद्द कर दी गई (radd kar di gai = was cancelled) stacks do + give + go. The compound कर देना (kar dena) survives inside the passive.

target: नई सड़क बनाई जा रही है।
english: A new road is being built.
tip: बनाई जा रही है (banai ja rahi hai = is being built) is feminine throughout to match सड़क (sadak = road) – both parts of a Hindi passive agree with the subject.

target: यह पुल पिछले साल बनाया गया था।
english: This bridge was built last year.
tip: Hindi builds the passive with जाना (jana = to go): बनाया गया था (banaya gaya tha = was built) is literally 'built went was'. The 'go' verb, not 'be', is what makes it passive.

target: चोर पुलिस द्वारा पकड़ा गया।
english: The thief was caught by the police.
tip: द्वारा (dwara = by) marks who did it: पुलिस द्वारा (pulis dwara = by the police). It's formal, news-report Hindi – everyday speech usually just doesn't name the doer.

target: सचिन को सर्वश्रेष्ठ खिलाड़ी चुना गया।
english: Sachin was chosen as the best player.
tip: There's no word for 'as': सर्वश्रेष्ठ खिलाड़ी चुना गया (sarvashreshth khiladi chuna gaya) is just 'best player was chosen' – the role sits bare next to the verb.
